title: Resource Pool

validation.research: Seven primary references: Kircher and Jain’s original Pooling paper; Apache Commons Pool GenericObjectPool and PooledObjectFactory APIs; SQLAlchemy connection pooling; Microsoft ObjectPool; official Python Condition and contextmanager documentation. The original paper explicitly names Resource Pool as a synonym, distinguishes object-only pooling and caching by resource identity, and describes reuse, initialization/anonymity and synchronized acquisition. Its full ten-page author-hosted PDF was retrieved at the published HTTP address after HTTPS certificate validation failed; relevant definitions, roles, implementation policy and related-pattern text were read. The article links the verified working address, and the primary documentation independently corroborates borrow/reset/validation/destruction, retained-versus-total allocation limits and reset-on-return qualifications. Pooling is preserved as an alias; Object Pool is described as the narrower object-based form. The buffer model, byte limits, guarded handle, close policy, code and diagrams are original teaching material.

runnable_example.verification: Exact five-line demo output; positive integer size and immutable 0/8-byte and binary payload boundaries, invalid inputs preserving contents, copied reads, eager physical resource count, and no pool-created worker; same backing resource receives a fresh guarded handle while old public read/write reject even during reuse; previous immutable read copies remain unchanged rather than claiming secure erasure; ordinary and BaseException job failures propagate while reset/return still occur, and repeated context exit does not double-return; real Condition instrumentation proves exhausted checkout waits, releases/reacquires the lock, and rechecks after an extra notification; real bytearray instrumentation gates reset outside the availability lock, keeps the slot unavailable, invalidates the old handle before reset, and verifies both open-pool republication and close-during-reset dropping; close wakes three blocked borrowers, preserves two active borrows until return, rejects new checkout, and does not republish returned buffers; four real callers perform 120 uses at size one and another 120 at size two, verifying no overlapping resource ownership, fixed physical inventory, clean contents at checkout, isolated writes, and stale-handle rejection; independent pool inventories/locks/close flags, final zeroed idle buffers, repeated close and all caller-thread joins return thread inventory to baseline. Instrumentation wraps real Condition/bytearray seams without replacing article pool methods. Assumes trusted nonshared handles and successful allocation/fixed cleanup; no broken-resource replacement, external-handle disposal, secure wipe of copies, deadline, forced reclamation, fairness or join-borrowers API is inferred.

example_limits: Original Python 3.11+ fixed pool of eager eight-byte bytearrays; the example demonstrates coordination rather than a claimed speed benefit for cheap memory allocation. Positive integer size sets the physical resource inventory. A real Condition protects idle availability and closure; while loops recheck after waiting/extra notifications. Each scoped borrow gets a fresh public-method guard over one exclusive backing array. Writes accept immutable 0–8-byte data and pad to eight bytes; reads return immutable copies. Finally invalidates the handle, zeroes the array outside the condition lock while unavailable, then republishes only if open. Closed pools drop returned buffers, reject new borrows and wake blocked callers while active use remains valid until scope exit. Tests verify ordinary/BaseException propagation with cleanup, stale guards during reuse, no double return on repeated context exit, reset gating and close races, three woken waiters with two active borrows, independent pools, and 240 concurrent uses across inventories one and two with all caller threads joined. Pool close itself does not join borrowers. Assumes allocation and fixed cleanup complete; clients are trusted not to bypass private state or share a handle concurrently. There is no failed-resource replacement, validation/disposal callback API, timeout, cancellation, fairness or forced reclamation. Clearing the bytearray does not erase existing returned copies or provide cryptographic secure-memory erasure. Real connections require backend-specific reset, compatibility, validation, retirement and failure policy; pool return does not decide commit or undo external effects.
